info.title: money
info.description: Budgeting and shared-expense tracking, API first, git-backed.

get.description:
Where this deployment's sign-in starts.

Computed server-side because only the server knows whether it is production or a preview;
the browser guessing its own prod origin from the hostname would be one more thing to
keep correct.

Complete a sign-in that production started on this preview's behalf.

The ticket is checked against *this* deployment's own hostname, so a ticket minted for
`pr-42` is useless at `pr-43` even though both trust the same signing key.

post.summary: Exchange an approved device code for an API key
post.description:
Returns `pending` until the user approves in their browser.

On approval this mints a *money* API key rather than handing the CLI the GitHub token,
so revoking CLI access never means revoking GitHub access.

get.description:
Every linked budget whose repo GitHub says the caller can read.

Budgets they cannot read are omitted, not reported as forbidden.

post.summary: Connect a GitHub repo as a budget

put.description:
Replaces the list wholesale, so removals are expressible and not just additions.

Membership decides who can be assigned a share, not who can reach the budget — that is
GitHub repo access. Someone listed here without repo access simply never signs in.

get.description: Defaults to the calling user's own envelopes, since buckets are per person.

post.description:
Records a git tag naming the commit the month ended on.

A tag rather than a field: it can be checked out to see the month exactly as it stood,
and it touches no file that a later edit would rewrite. Closing does not lock anything —
it is a bookmark, not a permission.

Assign to many buckets in one action, which is the payday case.

Funding envelopes one at a time is the single most repeated chore in envelope budgeting.
Three strategies cover it: top every bucket up to its target, or repeat what was assigned
or spent last month.

This deliberately does not stop when the money runs out. Ready-to-assign is allowed to go
negative, and the month view says so — refusing the assignment would leave the plan
half-applied and harder to reason about than an overcommitment you can see.

post.summary: Move money from one bucket to another
post.description:
Take from one envelope and give to another, in one action.

Covering an overspend by editing two assignment figures means doing the arithmetic
yourself and leaving the budget briefly wrong between the two saves. This does both sides
together and refuses to move more than the source actually holds.

put.summary: Create or update one of your buckets

post.summary: Record a payment between two people
post.description:
A settlement moves both net positions and touches no envelope.

`payer` defaults to the calling user but may name the other party. The person who is
*owed* is usually the one holding the phone when the money arrives, and if their partner
does not use the app nobody could otherwise record it. The caller must be one of the two
parties, so this records payments you were involved in, not other people's.

get.description:
Payees from this budget's own history, with the amount and bucket usually used.

Typing a shop's name in full every time is the slowest part of logging an expense, and
the answer is already in the ledger. Ranked by how recently *and* how often a payee was
used: a shop visited weekly should beat one visited once a year, but a one-off from
yesterday should still be reachable.

put.summary: Write the long-form note for an entry
put.description: Markdown in `notes/<entry-id>.md`, so a paragraph of context diffs line by line.

post.summary: Show how an entry would be split, without saving it
post.description: Answers "what will this rule do?" before anything is committed.

get.summary: Default split rules, in match order

put.description:
Replaces the list wholesale, because order is meaningful: first match wins.

Editing one rule in place would leave the caller unable to express a reordering.

post.description: The token is returned once here and never again; only its hash is stored.

get.summary: Repos you could connect as a budget
get.description:
Lists the caller's repos, flagging which already look like a budget.

"Looks like a budget" means it has a `budget.yaml`. That is checked for the most recently
pushed repos only — one API call each — and everything else is still listed, just without
the flag. Guessing wrong is cheap: connecting a repo without one fails with a clear error.

get.summary: Find a GitHub user to invite
Who has access to the data repo
get.description:
Repo access is the real permission model, so this shows it directly.

Pending invitations are included: without them someone just invited does not appear at
all, and it looks as though the invitation failed.

post.summary: Invite someone to the budget's data repo
post.description:
Sends a real GitHub invitation, and adds them to the budget's member list.

Both halves are needed and they are not the same thing: the invitation is what lets them
sign in at all, and membership is what lets them hold a share of an entry. Doing only the
first was the old behaviour, and it left people able to log in to a budget that could not
reference them.

get.description:
What each recurrence owes the ledger, up to `through` (default: two weeks out).

Dates already posted are excluded, so opening this twice never offers the same charge
twice. A paused recurrence is skipped entirely.

post.summary: Turn a due recurrence into a real entry
post.description:
Creates the entry and records that this date was posted, in one commit.

One commit matters: if the entry landed and the marker did not, the same charge would be
offered again and posted twice.

get.summary: Everything that has changed, newest first
get.description:
One feed for every change, whichever file it touched.

Assignments show up next to entries because they are the same kind of event to the person
reading — money moved — even though one lives in a ledger file and the other in a map.

post.description:
Revert a change, defaulting to your most recent un-reverted one.

Scoped to your own changes: in a shared budget, silently reversing your partner's work
from your phone is the failure worth designing against. Naming a sha reverts anyone's,
which makes doing so deliberate.

Re-apply the change your last undo reversed, by reverting the revert.

Only available while the undo is still your most recent change. Anything done afterwards
clears it, the way a new edit clears an editor's redo stack — re-applying a change on top
of later work would produce a state nobody asked for.

get.description:
Names the shop someone is standing in, so the first visit does not need typing.

Proxied rather than called from the browser, so the API key stays on the server. Returns
an empty list rather than an error when the lookup fails — a places outage should not
stop anyone recording an expense.

get.summary: A guessed entry, with its reasoning
get.description:
What this person probably about to record, drawn only from this budget's own history.

Every field the caller already knows narrows the pool the rest is drawn from, so filling
in the payee improves the amount and the split rather than being ignored.

LineItem.title: LineItem
LineItem.description:
One line on a receipt.

A receipt is one payment but several things bought, and they do not always belong in the
same envelope or to the same person — a supermarket run is groceries and a bottle of wine.
Splitting the *entry* cannot express that, because the entry's split is about the total.

A line carries its own shares when it needs to. When it does not, it simply belongs to
whatever the entry as a whole decided.

Place.title: Place
Place.description:
Where a payment happened.

Coordinates are committed to the budget repo, which is a deliberate choice: it makes the
suggestions work on every device and survive clearing a browser. It also means the repo
holds a durable, shared record of where you have been — see specs/data-model.md.

Recurrence.title: Recurrence
Recurrence.description:
How often something repeats.

Three cadences cover what a household actually has: a salary and rent monthly, a cleaner
weekly, insurance yearly. More exotic rules can be added when something real needs one.

Scheduled-Input.title: Scheduled
Scheduled-Input.description:
A template plus a recurrence: rent, a salary, a subscription.

It holds the same two-sided split an entry does, so posting one produces an ordinary
entry with nothing inferred at post time. `last_posted` is what stops the same charge
being offered twice.
